items.title: Day 4 Overview — Tasks & Competencies
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 4: The Calendar (Part 1 of 2)

Day 4 Overview

The Calendar is Outlook's biggest, most feature-rich element — today you'll view it, fill it with appointments and meetings, and set things up to repeat automatically. Tomorrow finishes the chapter with sharing and printing.

Competencies Covered Today

  • Use calendar views
  • Create and edit appointments and meetings
  • Set recurring appointments

Today's Tasks

  1. Watch the Chapter 4 Presentation (covers the whole chapter — today's viewing is the Calendar-views and Appointments/Meetings sections)
  2. Viewing the Calendar — read, then complete Hands-On OU4-D1 & D2
  3. Appointments and Meetings — read, then complete Hands-On OU4-D3–D8
No quiz today

Chapter 4's Self-Assessment Quiz and Test cover the whole chapter, so they're held until Day 5 (Part 2 of 2), after Sharing and Printing are covered.

items.title: Viewing the Calendar — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book pages: 61-66 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Use calendar views

The Calendar

Note: Outlook technically treats appointments and meetings as two different kinds of items — the main difference being that meetings let you include other people. In this course, "appointment" is used loosely to mean any scheduled calendar event, whether or not anyone else is invited.

Viewing the Calendar

Outlook offers several ways to look at your schedule: Day, Work Week (Monday-Friday only, by default), Week, Month, and Schedule view, plus a "Next 7 Days" option.

{{img:pg 62.png|Textbook page 62 — an annotated Week view, calling out the forward/back week buttons, the Weather bar, today's heading, the current-time line, and how Work Week view grays out non-work hours}}

Peeking at the Calendar

Just like peeking at People, you can peek at your calendar — hover over Calendar on the Navigation bar and a popup shows the current month plus anything on your schedule for the next seven days. Hovering directly over an appointment on the calendar itself shows an inline card with its Start, End, Location, and Reminder details.

Day View

Day view shows every event for one day; scroll bars move through the hours, and you can set your own start/end times instead of the 8:00 AM-5:00 PM default. It can also show your daily tasks at the bottom, if you turn that option on. The forward/back arrows move one day at a time (in Week or Month view, the same arrows move one week/month at a time instead).

Week and Work Week View

These are the views to check for open time in the current week. Work Week defaults to Monday-Friday, but you can change which days count as your work week in Options. Next 7 Days is similar, but always shows a rolling week starting today (including Saturday/Sunday) instead of the calendar week.

Month View

Month view shows the whole month at a glance — handy for spotting open dates, and it's the easiest view for dragging an appointment from one day to another.

{{img:pg 64.png|Textbook page 64 — a full Month view with recurring and one-off appointments visible across the grid}}

Schedule View

Schedule view lays your day out left-to-right instead of top-to-bottom — useful when you're comparing multiple people's calendars side by side to find a meeting time that works for everyone.

Changing Calendar Options

Calendar settings live in File → Options → Calendar — the most common change is your daily work hours, since not everyone works a traditional Monday-Friday, 8-to-5 schedule anymore. You can also change the default reminder time (15 minutes out of the box).

Adding Holidays, Time Zones & the Weather Bar

Outlook can add holidays to your calendar so you don't accidentally schedule over one — or, if you'd rather not clutter your own calendar, you can display a separate holiday calendar side by side instead. If you regularly work with someone in another time zone, you can add a second time zone to the calendar display. And the Weather bar shows a short forecast for your location (or up to five saved locations, switchable from a drop-down) right on the calendar — handy since weather can affect travel plans tied to your schedule.

items.title: Hands-On OU4-D1 & D2: Explore Calendar Views & Set Options
items.description:
Book pages: 65-66 · Develop Your Skills OU4-D1 & OU4-D2

Hands-On OU4-D1 & D2: Explore Calendar Views & Set Options

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — OU4-D1: Switch Calendar Views

  1. Click Calendar on the Navigation bar, then double-click a day about one week from today.
  2. Choose Home → Day to switch to Day view.
  3. Choose Home → Next 7 Days.
  4. Choose Home → Month.

Part 2 — OU4-D2: Set Calendar Options

  1. Choose File → Options → Calendar.
  2. Change your Start time to 7:30 AM and your End time to 4:30 PM (or whatever hours actually match your own schedule — the point is knowing where this setting lives).
  3. Click OK.
What to submit

Two screenshots: (1) your calendar in Month view; (2) the Outlook Options → Calendar tab showing your changed Start/End work hours before clicking OK.

items.title: Appointments and Meetings — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book pages: 67-77 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objectives: Create and edit appointments and meetings / Set recurring appointments

Appointments and Meetings

Both are created in your calendar whenever you need time blocked out — a doctor's visit, a client meeting, focused work time. The difference: an appointment is only on your own schedule; a meeting invites other people. You can quickly create an appointment by clicking a day/time and typing directly, or open the full New Appointment window to set the time, location, reminder, notes, and more.

Tip: you can convert any appointment into a meeting just by inviting attendees — add their email address(es) to the To field the same way you would a message (note: meeting invitations can't be sent as Cc or Bcc). The recipient then responds, and you can check who's accepted or declined.

Creating an Appointment

Click Calendar on the Navigation bar, then either double-click the starting time/day you want or click New Appointment on the Ribbon. Once created, the appointment's title and a shaded block show its duration on the calendar; an all-day or multi-day event instead displays as a banner across the top of the day(s) it spans.

{{img:pg 67.png|Textbook page 67 — a two-hour appointment shown as a shaded time block, and a multi-day event shown as a banner spanning three days}}

Editing an Appointment

Open any appointment to change its date, time, reminder, category, or privacy. You can type a time directly into the appointment window instead of only picking from the half-hour increments in the dropdown (8:15 AM, 11:11 AM — whatever you need). You can also just drag an appointment to a new time or day right on the calendar, which is fastest for moving something within the same week.

Setting a Reminder

Every new appointment gets a 15-minute reminder by default, but you can change it per appointment — 15 minutes might be plenty for a coworker down the hall, while a big presentation might call for a reminder a day or two ahead.

Choosing a Room

For meetings that need a boardroom or conference room, you can type the location directly, or pick from a list of rooms your organization has already set up (this books the room and warns other people it's taken, cutting down on double-booking).

How Appointments Are Shown

Coworkers can see your calendar based on what you've shared and your organization's settings, but the Show As setting works independently of that — it tells people whether you're available at a glance. New appointments default to Busy; you might switch a smaller appointment to Free so people still know they can reach you if something important comes up. The other options are Working Elsewhere, Tentative, and Out of Office.

Recurring Appointments

A recurring appointment repeats on a set pattern — the same day/time every week, every month, or whatever interval you choose — and Outlook creates every instance for you at once instead of one at a time.

Editing Recurring Appointments

You can edit just one occurrence, or the entire series at once. Editing the whole series applies your change to every instance.

Deleting a Recurring Appointment

Same choice applies to deleting — one occurrence or the whole series. Warning: once you delete a recurring appointment (an occurrence or the whole series), you cannot undo it — there's no getting it back.

{{img:pg 72.png|Textbook page 72 — the "Open Recurring Item" dialog, asking whether to open just one occurrence or the entire series}}

Turning an Email into an Appointment

If an email has information you'd rather track on your calendar than dig back through your inbox for, drag the message onto the Calendar link on the Navigation bar — Outlook creates a new appointment with the subject line as the title and the email's text copied into the appointment body automatically.

Creating a Meeting

Creating a meeting works almost exactly like creating an appointment — the only real difference is you send it as a request via email so it appears on every invited person's calendar too.

Meeting Organizers

Whoever creates a meeting is its organizer, and the meeting lives on that person's calendar — only people with editing rights to the organizer's calendar can change it, and the organizer role can't be handed off to someone else. (If someone else needs to take over, the practical fix is creating a brand-new meeting on their own calendar and deleting the original.) Meetings can recur too, in which case every future instance stays on the organizer's calendar. If an attendee edits their own copy of a meeting instead of waiting for the organizer to update it, that copy falls out of sync and won't receive the organizer's future updates.

Responding to Meetings

An invitation arrives as an email with four response choices: Accept, Tentative, Decline, or Propose New Time. Accepting or marking tentative adds it to your calendar; you can also choose whether to actually send your response back to the organizer — courteous for a small meeting, unnecessary (and unwanted) for one with hundreds of invitees.

{{img:pg 76.png|Textbook page 76 — the meeting-response send options (Edit the Response before Sending / Send the Response Now / Do Not Send a Response), and the Invite Attendees button that turns an existing appointment into a meeting}}

Note: once you respond to a meeting invitation, the original invite email disappears from your Inbox — from then on, you'll find the meeting on your Calendar instead.

Turning an Appointment into a Meeting

Any appointment can become a meeting after the fact — just click Invite Attendees on its Ribbon. The window's title and the Ribbon itself change to the meeting-scheduling layout once you do.

items.title: Hands-On OU4-D3–D8: Create, Edit, Repeat & Send Appointments
items.description:
Book pages: 68-77 · Develop Your Skills OU4-D3 through OU4-D8

Hands-On OU4-D3–D8: Create, Edit, Repeat & Send Appointments

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — OU4-D3: Create an Appointment

  1. Choose Home → New Appointment.
  2. Title: Planning Meeting for Silver Creek Oaks (or your own title).
  3. Set the Start Time to Thursday of next week, 1:00 PM and the End Time to 3:00 PM.
  4. Save & Close.

Part 2 — OU4-D4: Edit the Appointment

  1. Double-click the appointment from Part 1.
  2. Location: Conference Room.
  3. Show As: Tentative.
  4. Reminder: 30 minutes.
  5. Save & Close.

Part 3 — OU4-D5: Create a Recurring Appointment

  1. Choose Home → New Appointment. Title: Quarterly Budget Meeting. Start: 9:00 AM; End: 12:15 PM (pick any real upcoming date).
  2. Click Make Recurring, choose Monthly, then "The first Monday of every 3 months," and click OK.
  3. Save & Close.

Part 4 — OU4-D6: Edit the Entire Recurring Series

  1. Double-click the Quarterly Budget Meeting and choose The entire series.
  2. Change the Reminder to 2 days.
  3. Click Edit Recurrence, change the End time to 12:00 PM, and set the series to End after 4 occurrences. Click OK.
  4. Save & Close.

Part 5 — OU4-D7: Turn an Email into an Appointment

  1. Click Mail on the Navigation bar, then pick any email in your Inbox.
  2. Drag it down onto the Calendar icon on the Navigation bar and drop it.
  3. Set a start date/time and type Conference Room as the location.
  4. Save & Close. (Notice the title auto-filled from the email's subject, and the email text is now in the appointment body.)

Part 6 — OU4-D8: Create & Send a Meeting

  1. Click Calendar, then choose Home → New Meeting.
  2. Title: Press Release Party (or your own).
  3. Required: invite at least one classmate or your instructor, using their real VACE email address.
  4. Start Time: next Friday, 5:00 PM; End Time: 9:00 PM.
  5. Location: Silver Creek Oaks (or your own).
  6. Message body: "Let's celebrate together!" (or your own note).
  7. Click Send.
What to submit

Four screenshots: (1) the edited Planning Meeting appointment showing its Location, Show As, and Reminder from Parts 1-2; (2) the Quarterly Budget Meeting's recurring series settings after Part 4's edits; (3) the appointment created from a dragged email in Part 5; (4) the sent Press Release Party meeting from Part 6, showing your invited attendee(s).
